A line from Goethe for the Goethe year:
We have nothing with which to compare it.
Above all, compare this very line, which has been made so painfully embarrassing.
The most important sentence in Thomas Hobbes remains:

The power of such a sentence continues to operate even when, within the conceptual system being built, it is pushed to the edge or apparently even placed outside the system altogether. This pushing-aside is analogous to the way Christ is turned into a cult object by Dostoevsky’s Grand Inquisitor.

Hobbes states openly and argues scientifically for what Dostoevsky’s Grand Inquisitor actually does: he neutralizes the effect of Christ in the social and political sphere. He removes the anarchic force from Christianity. But in the background he still leaves Christianity with a certain legitimating effect and, in any case, refuses to give it up altogether.
A clever tactician gives up nothing unless it has become completely useless.
Christianity had not yet reached that point.
Who is closer to Dostoevsky’s Grand Inquisitor—the Roman Church,
or the sovereign of Thomas Hobbes?
Reformation and Counter-Reformation turn out to move in related directions.
Tell me who your enemy is, and I will tell you who you are.
The enemy is our own question made visible as a figure.
To separate the wolf’s hunting instinct from its hunger: abstract hunting instinct and abstract hunger.
To separate the drive toward knowledge—the search for truth—from the drive toward satisfaction through arriving at the correct answer.
Between Stalin organs and phosphorus bombs, for us Germans there remained only the fearful choice.
Upon the foreheads of the victims of fascism shines their transfigured light.
Only hopes without ulterior purpose have the power to draw toward themselves what they hope for.
In German, you cannot even say “thank you” politely without risking giving an insulting kind of “thanks.”

But how sad and depressing it becomes when a lyric poet takes himself onto the public stage, externalizes what is effortlessly present into dialectical-dialogical representation, and tries to make us take a dramatic interest in the prima-donna problems of a Tasso-like existence.

From 1933 to 1936 I felt so infinitely superior to those <…> poor thieves who were seizing power that even then my personal problem became identical with the general ontological question of the relation between spirit and mass, idea and interest.
“In such cases, the idea has always embarrassed itself,” Friedrich Engels said.
He seemed to fear this humiliation. He tried to avoid it. I did not fear it. I did not even think about it. That is why it cannot kill me today.

The general concern for humanity and the general convention called “humanism” can probably be explained physiologically. It comes from the feeling that human physical nature itself is now being mortally threatened by technology and natural science.
The homme machine—man as machine—is becoming serious now: syringes, injections, prostheses.
And so they cry out in desperation:
Stop the thief! But how can this concept, violated and debased long ago, still help us? It serves only as a pretext for moral outrage.
A pretext for constructing “crimes against humanity.”
In other words, only a basis for new criminalizations and new declarations that the political enemy stands outside the law.

Even with the best will in the world, one cannot deny it: the final word spoken by this most noble princess, this incarnation of German idealist spirit in Tasso and of German genius-worship— her final word is, after all: Away!
(Tasso, Act V, Scene 1.) That is the final word of German Idealism as a whole.
Kleist experienced it. He went to his death, into the sensual pleasure of the grave, with a poor woman. But the lady leaves the stage with a decisive:
Away! And she does not return.
Qui n’a pas l’esprit de son âge, de son âge a tout le malheur.

Whoever does not possess the spirit of his age suffers all the misfortune of his age. But âge here means “age” in several senses: one’s personal age, one’s stage of life, one’s historical age, even an entire world-age.
French leaves all of this open.

Where does this strange universal agreement on the word “humanism” come from? It comes from anxiety about the last remnant of nature that technology has not yet destroyed and replaced: the human body itself.
Fear that the body will now actually become a machine,
something whose parts can be altered or exchanged through drugs, vitamins, and replacements.
And so, full of fear, they cry:
Man! But the man they are calling upon has already been lost.
Hobbes was the archetype of internal emigration. All the great figures of the seventeenth century withdrew into esoteric thought. In that sense, he was authentic.
The clear precision of Hobbes’s language confirms his own philosophy of language in his own case: homo verbo fit potentior—man becomes more powerful through words.
But the English rejected Hobbes and cast him out.
Hobbes calls the Israelites a gens prophetarum avida—a people greedy for prophets (De Cive, Part III, ch. XVI, § 15, p. 312 of the Elzevir edition of 1647).
Above all, there is the classic passage on p. 343:

Non enim potest civis privatim determinare quis amicus, quis hostis publicus sit—a private citizen cannot decide for himself who is a friend and who is a public enemy. That passage belongs at the beginning of every study of the individual’s direct standing under international law.
The twin brotherhood of pacifism and Malthusianism; the united front of abortionists, advocates of cremation, and pacifists; the bodily sensibility of the women of the Anglo-Saxon elite.
Homer Lea, The Day of the Saxon, 1912.
A magnificent sentence: the world today is smaller than the Tower of Babel.
Said in 1912, long before the airplane and radio!
Homer Lea, a harbinger of the revolution in space.
The earth is smaller than the Tower of Babel, and within this cramped space the confusion of languages becomes all the more deadly.
America + Russia; colonial war + civil war. That is the reality behind the return of the just war.

The basic line of thought: from chaos to cosmos; from the state of nature to the state. But at the point of transition there is always the man of force, the man who makes the transition happen: Hercules, who kills the monsters and is then left behind as the final monster himself. That is what this “state” is.
“When culture arrives, the heroes disappear,” says Hegel.
But this culture has become stale to us. This peace is beginning to bore me. So we call for heroes.
What was the heart of the interstate jus publicum Europaeum? The overcoming of civil war and the exclusion of colonial war!
And what does the return of the just war, brought about by America and Russia, mean? It means turning war between states back into colonial war and civil war.
Only hopes that are free of intention can attract what is hoped for.
Free of intention—that is, giving up every deliberate hope: sperans contra spem, hoping against hope, a hope that expects nothing.
Expectation from no sources of law.
In the past, recognition as a state under international law—that is, under the jus publicum Europaeum—meant recognition as a justus hostis, a lawful enemy.
Today, after the introduction of the just war, it no longer means that. So it means nothing at all.

The German language is full of mysterious acts of generation and self-generation. For example, I describe a real situation when I say:

Today, means become immediate. They do not become ends in themselves, because there are no ends anymore. They simply become immediate. There are only drives and functions. So what are we supposed to do?

Give up every intention and surrender ourselves to the current, without even deciding whether the current carrying us along is like a river such as the Nile, or an electric current made up of waves and lines of force.
Every German word produces a shifting echo. It lacks an image, searches for an image, and wavers between images.
Kleist sought the sensual pleasure of the grave, the bed of the Empress.

His suicide was not heroic conduct directed against his own personality (compare Hegel, Addition to § 70 of the Philosophy of Right). Nor was protest against the political situation the decisive thing. His act was not meant to claim some higher right.
After the ending of Penthesilea, it was really only consistent.
The deed itself was simply the ripe fruit growing from the tree of a feeling that knew with complete certainty.
Just look at this porcelain-factory world of Goethe’s Tasso or his Iphigenia!
It simply has to end with an “Away!”
Everything here is so infinitely refined and cultivated that people can only whisper in blank verse and live on nothing but nectar and ambrosia.
At last, the genius falls out of character and receives the well-deserved classical command:
“We have nothing with which to compare it!”

A beautiful subject for the Goethe Year, with E. R. Curtius as the custodian of high culture, defending the humanist cult-image of Goethe with all the zeal of a churchwarden and all the quotation-covered pedantry of a schoolmaster.
